accuracy.evidence: Poles as the ends of the spin axis (90° N and 90° S) and the Equator at 0°, equidistant from both, checked against National Geographic Education 'North Pole', 'South Pole' and 'Equator' entries; colder towards the poles because low-angle sunlight spreads the same beam over more ground and through more atmosphere, with ice reflecting much of it (Met Office 'Why are the poles cold?'); Earth–Sun distance not the cause; South Pole annual mean about −49 °C (British Antarctic Survey / Amundsen–Scott records); polar bears in the Arctic, emperor penguins round Antarctica, no wild penguins in the Arctic.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report at KS1: the South Pole is hot because it is 'at the bottom' (walk prediction, p5, tag south); the Equator is a real line or near the top (belt prediction, challenge tag real and belt); the middle is a pole (find step 'Tap the middle' button with its own feedback, tag mid); the poles are cold because they are far from the Sun (sun prediction, m4, tag far); penguins and polar bears live together (who prediction, m6, tag bear).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagglobe is built on a drawn globe: tap targets at the exact top and bottom of the circle, an Equator ring whose height is dragged while two arrows compare its distance to each pole, an explorer dragged along the axis with a thermometer that falls with distance from the Equator, and five parallel Sun rays whose hit points on the circle bunch up at the middle and spread near a pole. It shares no mechanism with flagpoles (magnets), flagpolaran (adaptations) or flagseaneed; the lab_distinct gate measured at most 3% overlap with any other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found before it is named: tapping the middle draws a ring and says it is near the Equator, not a pole; the two distance arrows only match when the belt sits halfway, and the label switches from 'North Pole nearer' to 'halfway'; the thermometer falls on the way to either pole and the South Pole visit says the bottom is freezing too; the ray dots visibly spread when the Sun is aimed near a pole, with the earlier middle dots kept faintly for comparison.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions with tempting wrong options: 'in the middle' / 'on the side' for the North Pole, 'round the top of the Earth' for the Equator, 'hot' for the South Pole, 'they are much further from the Sun' for why the poles are cold, and 'yes, both at the North Pole' for polar bears and penguins. Each is tested by the task that follows, and the reveal line names the prediction and the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions (where the South Pole is, what the Equator is, coldest places, why the poles are cold, walking from the Equator, where penguins live, distance of each pole from the Equator). Wrong options carry tags mid, flip, belt, real, south, far, same and bear, each with its own message, e.g. 'The poles are not much further from the Sun. Its rays hit them slanting and spread out, so they warm less.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid and adult readability limits (adult was rewritten from FK 10.7 into shorter sentences to pass). Kid sentences are short and concrete ('The very top of it is the North Pole.'); globe, Equator and pole are each explained in plain words when first used. Young-mode buttons are 56 px tall with larger text.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: where the poles are, what the Equator is, colder away from it, why (slanting sunshine). Adult: KS1 geography link and key words, the mechanism with the −49 °C figure, five named mistakes, then exactly what the lab does. No filler pattern matched and the 12% duplicate gate passed against 369 Day, Night and the Seasons and 645 Polar Animals.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android dark, iPhone 13 light and desktop screenshots of every step after Show me. The globe was moved down (centre at max(43% of height, radius + 80 px)) after the first pass showed the status line overlapping the North Pole label; the explorer now walks beside the axis so it no longer hides the pole labels; the feedback strip sits below the South Pole label at both sizes.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin: 'Tap the very top' / 'Tap the middle' / 'Tap the very bottom', 'Move the belt up/down', 'Walk north/south', 'Shine on the middle / near the North Pole / near the South Pole', and one button per part of the globe for each animal. The canvas aria-label and live region carry every message, including the explorer's temperature word. walk.cjs passed axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; real pointer taps and drags were also tested on every step.
